articles.title: Burnham defends Jackdaw decision as Badenoch urges PM to overturn ban on new oil and gas licences
articles.summary: The UK government says the field, which is opposed by environmental campaigners, could be producing gas by the end of this month.
articles.body:
The UK government has approved production from the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea amid intense debate about the project's environmental and economic impact.

Ministers said the first gas could be produced by the end of this month, helping heat millions of homes, and also announced the creation of a new energy wealth fund.

But environmental campaigners said the decision would hamper efforts to tackle climate change and make "no meaningful difference" to UK energy security.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch accused the prime minister of "dithering" on Jackdaw and said a ban on new oil and gas licences should be repealed - but Andy Burnham said her party had "messed up" the original decision.

Jackdaw is situated 150 miles (241km) east of Aberdeen and is operated by Adura, a joint venture between Shell and Norwegian state energy firm Equinor.

A decision is yet to be taken on whether production can begin at Rosebank, the UK's largest known untapped oil field, which is located off the coast of Shetland in the North Atlantic.

Adura says Jackdaw will provide about 6% of UK gas production, enough to power 1.4 million homes. After imports are included, that amounts to about 2% of total UK demand.

The gas will be pumped to the existing Shearwater platform for processing – known as a tie-back in industry terms – before being piped to the St Fergus gas terminal in Aberdeenshire.

The UK government said that over its expected 11-year lifespan, Jackdaw would support the UK's gas supply, protect hundreds of jobs and add £2.9bn to the economy.

Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said the gas from Jackdaw would be in homes and businesses this month - although she told BBC Radio Scotland Breakfast that it would not lower energy bills this winter.

She said the decision would "help minimise the UK's use of imported higher emission fuels as we continue our transition to renewables and nuclear".

"The decision is compatible with our legally binding climate commitments, and we remain resolute in ending new licences for oil and gas and achieving net zero by 2050," she said.

The UK government also announced the establishment of an energy wealth fund using tax revenue from oil and gas extraction, with an initial £2bn of funding, to invest in renewable and low carbon energy projects.

At Prime Minister's Questions, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch thanked Burnham for "finally" approving Jackdaw but accused the government of "dithering" over the decision.

She also urged Labour to repeal its ban on all new oil and gas licences.

"We have the resources, the expertise and the people. What we have lost is the confidence to make tough decisions," she said.

The prime minister said he had made a decision that the previous Tory government had "messed up".

He said they had got decisions wrong because they did not give any regard to climate obligations, and that "these things have to be considered in the round".

Burnham also said he had asked the chancellor and energy secretary to look into whether standing charges could be removed from gas bills.

Scotland's First Minister John Swinney said he hoped the announcement would provide some certainty for the north east of Scotland.

"It is vital that the economic benefits of our energy are felt here in Scotland and used to bring energy bills down, rather than flowing to the Treasury to plug more short-term spending gaps," said the SNP leader.

He also welcomed the creation of an energy wealth fund, which he said should be "prioritised for offshore renewable opportunities and be ringfenced to be focused on the north east of Scotland".

Scottish Conservative leader Russell Findlay said the decision was a victory for Scotland's oil and gas workers, but added: "They should never have had to wait this long for common sense to prevail."

Business leaders in Aberdeen said it was "exactly the sort of pragmatic call the North Sea has been crying out for", and unions also welcomed the decision.

But the co-leader of the Scottish Greens, Ross Greer, described the approval as "climate vandalism".

He said: "It is a devastating betrayal of our children's future and it won't even lower energy bills in the here and now."

Environmental campaigners argue that this summer's heatwaves demonstrate the need to tackle climate change by rejecting both Jackdaw and Rosebank.

Areeba Hamid, the co-executive director of Greenpeace, said approving Jackdaw was "the wrong decision" in terms of lowering energy bills, providing energy security, and addressing climate change.

Oxfam said the government had "drilled straight through the UK's climate commitments" and accused the prime minister of sending "the wrong signal as the impacts of climate change intensify".

The charity says the government must commit to not approving any new oil and gas licences, including the proposals for Rosebank.

Jackdaw sits close to the boundary between the British and Norwegian sectors of the North Sea, in an area where Westminster originally granted licences to explore for oil and gas in 1970 and 1989.

The field was discovered in 2005 but it was expensive and technically difficult to exploit.

Shell did not commit to its development until 2022, shortly after the Conservative government had granted consent for production.

But in January 2025, after a challenge by environmentalists, the Court of Session in Edinburgh ruled that consent for Jackdaw and Rosebank had been granted unlawfully .

The judge, Lord Ericht, said the developers should have provided a more detailed account of the fields' impact on climate change as part of the permitting process.

The judge allowed the companies to continue with preparatory work short of producing oil and gas while they crafted new environmental impact assessments taking into account the eventual effect of actually burning the fossil fuels, not just the emissions which would be created in extracting them.

When BBC News visited the platform this summer, Adura CEO Neil McCulloch said its approval was vital to avoid domestic supply shortages this winter.

However, the UK government has previously suggested that Jackdaw will have little impact on energy security and none on reducing domestic gas and electricity bills.

In August, in an interim response to a consultation on the future of the country's gas supplies, Energy Minister Michael Shanks said the UK would inevitably become more reliant on imports as domestic production declined .

"With diminishing output from the North Sea over the past decades, any gas produced from the UK Continental Shelf represents a tiny fraction of global demand and so will not lower prices nor materially boost supply," wrote Shanks.

UK government approves drilling in Jackdaw gas field with production to start this month

Chris Mason: Jackdaw approved but tricky energy trade-offs remain

What is happening with the Jackdaw and Rosebank gas and oil fields?

Labour has previously said it is opposed to the issuing of new exploration licences but it will consider new production projects if they are tied back to existing facilities.

McCulloch described the Jackdaw decision as "an important and positive step forward" - but said attention now turned to Rosebank.

He has urged the UK government to approve production from the field, in which Adura owns an 80% stake. The other 20% is held by London-based Ithaca Energy.

Rosebank contains an estimated 300 million to 500 million barrels of oil.

But while most of Jackdaw's gas is likely to be consumed in the UK, Rosebank's oil will be taken off by tanker and sold on international markets.

articles.title: Glee reboot: The US high school musical comedy-drama is to return on Hulu and Disney+
articles.summary: Ryan Murphy's popular musical comedy-drama is set to return on Hulu and Disney+ after a decade away.
articles.body:
We never stopped believin'... now it's official: Glee, the Emmy-winning US high school musical comedy drama, is set to return.

Ryan Murphy's series, which chronicled the highs and lows of choir members from Ohio, premiered on Fox in 2009 and ran for six seasons until 2015.

The original cast included Lea Michele, Amber Riley, the late Cory Monteith, Jane Lynch and Matthew Morrison as Will Schuester, the optimistic teacher leading the fictional McKinley High's glee club.

The reboot was announced by Disney and Hulu via the show's social media team on Wednesday.

The show was a huge hit first time around, known for its big laughs and big heart, tackling topics such as sexuality, race, disability and mental health.

In the series, glee club New Directions helped misfit students find their voices through song and dance.

Lynch served as the club's main antagonist, the villainous cheerleading coach Sue Sylvester.

The choir's covers of Don't Stop Believin', River Deep, Mountain High and Smooth Criminal also brought older hit songs to the attention of younger audiences.

In 2010, the show was adapted for a concert tour in which was captured on film.

Around the same time, the cast overtook The Beatles as the non-solo act with the most Billboard Hot 100 appearances.

On Wednesday, the Wanted singer Max George told BBC Scotland that appearing in the show's sixth season was "an amazing experience", adding that he'd "love to do it again".

"I messaged the casting director from it, just with wide eyes from the announcement," he said.

Asked if it makes sense for the series to come back, he said: "I think so… It's been over 10 years, so I think that's a nice break.

"I think it was probably coming towards the end in terms of the storylines and everything, but 10 years has gone by, and Ryan Murphy will probably come up with something genius. So I'm expecting big things."

In a recent interview with Entertainment Tonight, co-creator Murphy confirmed he had written a reboot script with collaborators Brad Falchuk and Ian Brennan.

He also said he had "been in touch with around 10 of the original cast members".

"It's very sweet, they all had a lot of questions but they all were very enthusiastic about the idea," he said. "Nobody's read it, so we'll see."

He added: "I vowed to myself that I wanted to write a couple of them to see what people think, particularly the cast, because we were very close when we were making it."

It came after Michelle, who played Rachel Berry, the ambitious singer at the centre of the club, had told E! News that she - like Lynch - would be more than happy to return.

"I will always love Glee," she said. "I love Ryan Murphy. It just holds such a special place in my heart for me... I will follow Ryan wherever he goes."

Speaking to Bustle recently, another star of the show, Chris Colfer, admitted that any such reboot would be difficult following the death of Naya Rivera , who played Glee club favourite Santana Lopez.

"It was a really tough show to do, and it would be really hard to do it now that Naya is gone," said Colfer, who portrayed Kurt Hummel - the flamboyant singer and original choir member who faces bullying at the school.

"But I do know that Glee fans would probably come after me with pitchforks and jazz hands if I said no. So I don't know, but hopefully I'll have more information and I can actually think about it."

Rivera died in 2020 at the age of 33 in an accidental drowning.

Hers was the third death among the Glee cast. Monteith, who played football star turned singer Finn Hudson, died in 2013 at the age of 31 from a toxic mix of alcohol and heroin.

Mark Salling, another Glee cast member, took his own life in 2018 at the age of 35 while awaiting sentencing on child pornography charges.

A mini Glee reunion occurred on Sunday at London's Royal Albert Hall, when Darren Criss, aka Glee's Blaine Anderson, brought out Colfer for a duet of the song Baby It's Cold Outside.

Earlier this month, former Glee co-stars Harry Shum Jr and Amber Riley reunited on Dancing with the Stars.

articles.title: Holocaust school lessons to be improved after 'shocking' antisemitism review
articles.summary: Education Secretary Lucy Powell has stressed the importance of reminding new generations of the horrors of the Holocaust.
articles.body:
Education Secretary Lucy Powell says the government will "update and strengthen" Holocaust education within schools after a major review highlighted the "shocking scale" of antisemitism in British society.

Schools and colleges in England will be required to recognise antisemitism as a distinct category of harm and take explicit action against it.

It means anti-Jewish hatred will be treated as a specific safeguarding risk rather than being dealt with through existing measures to stop racism and bullying.

The government has accepted all of the 27 recommendations made in the government-commissioned review including dedicated training for teachers and more consistent recording of incidents.

Schools should recognise antisemitism as distinct form of harm, review says

The review into antisemitism in schools and colleges in England was led by former Ofsted chief inspector Sir David Bell and presented to Parliament on Wednesday.

Powell told the BBC it marked a "generational moment" to re-educate young people, among whom she said the issue of antisemitism was "particularly prevalent".

She said: "It's definitely a crisis and I think it's actually got worse since Sir David began this review. This has become a real challenge for Jewish people in our country, but also Jewish students and Jewish teachers working in our schools and colleges.

"I do really feel it is a generational moment to educate this generation and the next – that is the job of education – to understand what antisemitism is in the modern world."

Speaking on Holocaust education, the education secretary said new lessons will "challenge" some of the concepts that young people have.

The review also calls for stronger guidance on political impartiality for teachers.

Powell told the House of Commons "teachers should not bring their own political views into the classroom" but they should not avoid discussing important topics.

The review was launched following a series of high-profile incidents including the attack at Heaton Park synagogue in Manchester in October 2025, in which two men were killed.

Separate reviews were also commissioned into antisemitism in healthcare and into public order and hate crime laws.

The BBC revealed in August that the Bell review had found Jewish schoolchildren were experiencing regular harassment and abuse.

It also found that headteachers of some Jewish schools were spending more of their time dealing with security arrangements than educational matters .

The review also recommends that the government sets up a type of hotline where school leaders can access immediate advice on tackling antisemitism.

Bell, who is now vice-chancellor of the University of Sunderland, heard evidence from pupils, teachers, governors and parents across state and independent schools, as well as from community organisations.

He told the BBC: "This is not just a report for Jewish children in Jewish schools. This is for all children and young people in all schools and colleges. We know that antisemitism crosses all boundaries."

Earlier this month, the BBC was given rare access inside a Jewish school in Hertfordshire, where pupils and staff operate under tight security, amid heightened concerns about antisemitism.

Spencer Lewis, the executive headteacher of Yavneh College, said that security was an "innate part" of his role.

"When you come in in the morning, there are high gates, high fences, lots of security cameras. We have four full-time security staff. And it sort of just becomes part of what you do," he said.

In response to the recommendations, the government will also encourage schools to adopt the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA)'s working definition of antisemitism, although it cannot make it compulsory.

The definition is supported by mainstream Jewish organisations and has been adopted by 47 countries, including the UK, as well as most British universities.

However, some of the IHRA definition's examples of antisemitic behaviour have proven controversial.

The Board of Deputies of British Jews said that adopting the IHRA definition would provide schools with a tool "to deepen understanding of contemporary antisemitism".

In a statement, a spokesperson told the BBC: "Treating antisemitism in schools as a safeguarding issue will have the benefit of creating an explicit duty on all schools to address this as they would any other threat to children's safety, and will strengthen accountability."

Rabbi Charley Baginksy and Rabbi Josh Levy, co-leads of the Movement for Progressive Judaism, said that the report "exposes serious failures in how schools recognise and respond to antisemitism".

They said: "Alongside that urgent question of how schools deal with hatred and educate about Jewish persecution, we also need to ensure they teach about Jewish creativity, music, literature, humour and the extraordinary pleasure of belonging to this diverse tradition."

Dan Green, Chief Executive of the Anne Frank Trust UK, said the review "confirms what we see in classrooms every day".

"Antisemitism in our schools is real, it is widespread, and too often it goes unrecognised and unchallenged."

"One-off assemblies are not enough, and neither is sitting pupils in front of a video. Young people need the space to ask difficult questions, challenge their own assumptions and understand that antisemitism did not start or end with the Holocaust."

The National Education Union raised concerns about creating a "hierarchy of racism" and adopting the IHRA definition.

It said the latter risked "blurring the line between antisemitism and legitimate criticism of the Israeli government and the genocide in Gaza".

The union welcomed a "strengthened focus on antisemitism" while underlining that "no form of racism should be minimised".

Recent figures from the Community Security Trust, an organisation which provides security advice and support to the Jewish community, showed a spike in antisemitic incidents at schools.

It found in the first half of 2026 that antisemitism in schools had reached the highest level ever recorded for the first six months of any year.

articles.title: Shrewsbury artist Doodle Boy to host first solo exhibition
articles.summary: Joe Whale was commissioned to doodle on the walls of a local restaurant at the age of nine.
articles.body:
A teenager who went viral after being commissioned to doodle on the wall of a restaurant is preparing to open his first solo exhibition.

Joe Whale, also known as the Doodle Boy, gained international attention at the age of nine, when his artwork appeared on the walls of Shrewsbury restaurant, Number Four.

Now 16, he has just returned to the UK from Australia for his Ambassadors of Feeling exhibition, which is due to open at London's Truman Brewery on Friday.

"What it's about is 10 key characters which each represent a key emotion in the human experience," Whale said. "Especially for me as I navigate my youth."

"Obviously my 13-year-old self, my nine-year-old self, all plays a part in that," he explained.

The exhibition, which is open until 25 October, will feature original paintings, sculptures and hand-painted jackets created in collaboration with fashion brand, Parajumpers.

Whale, who previously signed a deal with Nike, was once watched by England footballers when he created a mural in their honour, and has also produced artwork celebrating Charles Darwin .

The former pupil at St George's Junior School, who was once encouraged to stop doodling in class, has since collaborated with brands including Disney and M&S.

Whale, who moved to Adelaide in Australia with his family two years ago, described going overseas as the "biggest change" as "everything was new".

"My environment was new. I kind of took that change and transferred it to my artwork," he explained.

"I started using more colour, more character based stuff with more of an abstract theme. I started thinking more intentionally about the messaging and the meaning that I want to convey."

The illustrator, who said he had now left school to focus on his art, said it got to a point where he had to choose between the two.

"In Australia, how it works is year 12 is part of the high school because they start a year after," he told BBC Radio Shropshire.

"I've been in a wrestling match with my parents... they've let me come out of school and focus on my art."

The 16-year-old said he was also interested in fashion in the future, having recently attended Milan Fashion Week.

"It was a really good experience for me to be able to go into that environment", he said.

articles.title: 'Shouldn't have come if unwell': Subodh Uniyal defends public reprimand of Daler Mehndi
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Uttarakhand minister Subodh Uniyal on Wednesday defended himself over reprimanding singer Daler Mehndi on stage during an event, saying the
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Uttarakhand minister Subodh Uniyal on Wednesday defended himself over reprimanding singer Daler Mehndi on stage during an event, saying the artiste should not have performed if he was unwell.Speaking to news agency PTI, Uniyal said Mehndi was only lip-syncing during the event and that, as a public representative associated with the event's organising committee, he came under pressure from people who wanted the issue to be questioned."Daler Mehndi, being a big name, was invited to the Kunjapuri Fair. But during the performance, it became apparent that he was only lip-syncing and not singing. I, being a local representative and also associated with the organising committee, felt the pressure from people who wanted this to be questioned," Uniyal said."Mehndi was not able to speak or walk. At that point, I thought he was under the influence of some substance. I don't know what, because a medical examination was not conducted," he added.Uniyal said he later learnt that Mehndi was unable to speak because he was unwell."Being such a big artiste, he should have informed us about this. This fact was revealed only when he was interrupted. If he was unwell, he should not have come to perform," the minister said."We were asked to make full payment of Rs 35 lakh in advance to the artiste; hotels were also booked in advance. I have nothing personal against Mehndi nor any intention to hurt him, but such a big artiste, knowing his condition, should have refused to perform," Uniyal said."I stand by the fact that if an artiste's respect must stay intact, they should also work accordingly. I did not use any foul language while speaking to Mehndi," he added.The controversy erupted after Uniyal went on stage and expressed displeasure while Mehndi was performing at the Siddhpeeth Maa Kunjapuri Tourism and Development Fair, a cultural event organised by the Uttarakhand government at Narendra Nagar in the New Tehri area on Sunday night.Congress demands minister's apologyThe controversy also took on political overtones, with Congress demanding that Uniyal publicly apologise for the way the episode was handled.“The treatment meted out to Mehndi is deeply unfortunate and runs counter to Uttarakhand’s glorious tradition of hospitality,” Amarjit Singh, general secretary of the Uttarakhand Pradesh Congress Committee, said.Artists rally behind MehndiMeanwhile, several people from the entertainment industry, including actor Anupam Kher, stand-up comedian Vir Das and singers Shaan, Palash Sen, Gurdas Maan and Alisha Chinai, came out in support of Mehndi. They said the artiste, who has been singing for three decades, was unwell, did not drink and should have been treated with greater respect."Couple of days ago, I saw a video in which Daler Mehndi ji was singing on stage and some minister got up and spoke to him insultingly. I wasn't there so I don't know but I've known Daler ji for 25 to 30 years. I know that he does not drink and he is one of the finest human beings that I have met. I personally know that he has not been keeping well for two-three years," Kher said in a video on X on Wednesday."Nobody should speak to anybody like this and that also on a public forum. This is not fair. To publicly accuse someone like this is wrong. Daler ji I am so sorry," he added.Comedian Vir Das said his first international show was in Dubai at Mehndi's show."So not just music people, comedy people also have a lot to owe to this great man and this great artist. And he was humble, nice, supportive and amazing. Daler paaji, I hope you feel well in your corner. Thank you from a very young comedian," Das said on Instagram.Mehndi's brother, singer Mika Singh, confirmed that the artiste had undergone major surgery and challenged anyone to prove that his elder brother had ever consumed alcohol. Although there has been speculation about Mehndi's health, the nature of his illness and surgery remains unclear.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Trump says AI data centres should pay ‘dividends’ in pre-midterm shift
articles.summary: US president has continued to support data centres in advance of midterms, despite growing opposition from Republicans.
articles.body:
United States President Donald Trump has said AI data centres should pay “dividends” to communities, in a shift before the midterm elections.

“If companies want to make their Data Centers popular, pay the community, and/or individuals within the community, a ‘dividend'” Trump said in a post on Truth Social on Wednesday.

The president’s comments come after he doubled down on his support for data centres, a stance seen as one of several political liabilities for Republicans in the run-up to the midterm election, as Trump’s approval rating has hit record lows.

Polls show dismal support for such centres amid concerns about the sprawling complexes’ water and energy use.

In the post, Trump advised companies that they could make the centres popular if they “pay the community, and/or individuals within the community, a ‘dividend’.”

“I have watched the process closely, and Data Centers that were highly unpopular in a certain area, have become extremely popular when a financial deal is struck,” he said. “MAKE DEALS, and get them built!!!”

Several top Republican candidates have opposed data centres before the midterm polls, with the issue emerging as an area of rare bipartisan consensus in advance of the November 3 vote.

Republican Senate candidates, including Ken Paxton in Texas, Mike Rogers in Michigan and John Husted in Ohio, have all called for more restrictions and oversight on the centres, in a reversal of earlier positions.

The issue featured prominently in a recent debate in Iowa, where Republican Senate Candidate Ashley Hinson said the local level should decide whether to build AI data centres.

Despite the shifting sentiment, Trump in late August issued an impassioned defence of data centres, decrying what he called “the anti-Data Center movement” as a gift to China.

“The only reason that communities throughout the USA should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor,” Trump wrote at the time.

“If they want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let Data Reign.”

Trump has taken several measures to accelerate data centre development, including issuing an executive order last year that called for measures to fast-track permitting and environmental review. The order promised to use federal land for the “expeditious and orderly development of data centers”.

Trump has also backed a voluntary pledge by AI companies to cover the full cost of the electricity data centres use, but has avoided supporting legally binding federal restrictions.

A Gallup poll conducted in March suggested that 71 percent of Americans opposed establishing AI data centres in their areas.

An ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos poll released on Wednesday identified a similar rate of disapproval, with 72 percent of respondents saying that they opposed building new data centres in their communities.

articles.title: Larry David mocks socialists in satirical essay, drawing criticism over Israel jokes

articles.body: Comedian Larry David drew criticism from democratic socialists after writing a satirical essay mocking the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), its anti-Israel positions and political correctness, while a California political activist mocked those who took offense at the "Curb Your Enthusiasm" creator's humor. David's October 17 essay in Air Mail, titled "The View from Here," imagined the longtime Hollywood liberal joining the DSA and successfully proposing 12 increasingly over-the-top additions to the socialist organization's manifesto. DOZENS MISSING AFTER PASSENGER FERRY SINKS AS RESCUERS SCOUR SOUTH PACIFIC COASTLINE The pair had gone out for a fishing trip on Saturday, Oct. 10 — and have not been heard from since, according to reports. Barradell said the family is hoping for their safe return and is asking people who have been fishing or traveling in the area to share any information that could help. articles.title: Fred MacMurray raised cattle on his 1,750-acre California ranch; part of it, the 52-acre Flax Estate and Vineyard, now owned by Jeffrey Ubben and Laurie Ubben, lists for $22 million after their $21 million purchase in 2016
articles.summary: A 52-acre estate in California’s wine country, once part of Hollywood actor Fred MacMurray’s sprawling ranch where he raised Scottish Black Angus cattle,
articles.body: A 52-acre estate in California’s wine country, once part of Hollywood actor Fred MacMurray’s sprawling ranch where he raised Scottish Black Angus cattle, has hit the market for $22 million. Located in Healdsburg’s Russian River Valley, the property includes 26 acres of organically farmed Pinot Noir vineyards, three residences and interiors by renowned designer Ken Fulk. According to Mansion Global, the asking price also includes the furnishings.Known as Flax Estate and Vineyard, the property is owned by philanthropists and restaurateurs Jeffrey and Laurie Ubben, who purchased it in 2016 for $21 million. The estate was originally formed from three parcels of MacMurray’s 1,750-acre ranch, which dates back to 1941.Fred MacMurray’s former ranch has a Hollywood legacyMacMurray, who enjoyed a career spanning five decades, appeared in more than 100 films. His credits include Billy Wilder’s 1944 classic Double Indemnity and popular Disney films such as The Shaggy Dog and The Absent-Minded Professor. He also played Steve Douglas, the father in the sitcom My Three Sons, which aired from 1960 to 1972.During his ownership of the sprawling ranch, MacMurray raised Scottish Black Angus cattle. Today, a portion of that historic property has evolved into a working vineyard estate that combines its Hollywood past with modern country living.“Rarely do we see a property with so much provenance,” said Alain-Martin Pierret of Compass Healdsburg, who co-listed the estate with colleague Haley Skerrett. He described it as a “pedigree boutique vineyard” and compared the grounds to a private Yosemite Park.The vineyard operation is reportedly ready to continue under new ownership. Buyers also have the option of hiring DuMOL, the winery co-owned by the Ubbens, to manage the vineyard.Three homes, vineyard views and interiors by Ken FulkThe estate comprises three residences: a renovated 1940s farmhouse, a contemporary home and a rebuilt caretaker’s cottage. It also has direct access to the Russian River and includes an entertainment barn.The approximately 4,000-square-foot contemporary home stands among mature oak trees and features a distinctive white geometric design. It has four bedrooms, four full bathrooms and one half bathroom. Expansive glass walls frame views of Mount St. Helena and Fitch Mountain.“It feels like a giant treehouse,” Pierret said, describing the home’s natural light, large windows and connection to the surrounding landscape.The 1940s farmhouse offers approximately six bedrooms and bathrooms, along with a range of recreational amenities. These include a 75-foot swimming pool, a spa, a gym, a sauna, tennis and bocce courts, orchards, and flower and vegetable gardens.“It has a porch, a gigantic dining room and a family room,” Pierret said. He added that the two main homes offer distinctly different lifestyles and decor, allowing residents to experience two different settings within the same estate.The two-bedroom caretaker’s cottage was rebuilt by the Ubbens. The interiors across the property were designed by Ken Fulk, whose work adds to the estate’s appeal. The furnishings are included in the $22 million asking price.Estate served as a retreat for musicians, family and friendsThe Ubbens have used Flax Estate and Vineyard as both a private retreat and a gathering place for musicians. They have hosted singer-songwriters and bands performing at Little Saint, their farm-to-table vegan restaurant and music venue in Healdsburg.The property also became a refuge for family and friends during the Covid-19 pandemic. “During the pandemic, we housed New York City escapees, our kids and their friends, and 12 dogs,” Jeffrey Ubben said in a statement.Today, the estate continues to serve as a family gathering place, with the couple’s grandchildren enjoying the grounds and picking grapes from the vines, according to Ubben.Who are the owners Jeffrey Ubben and Laurie Ubben?Jeffrey Ubben is the co-founder of San Francisco-based investment management firm ValueAct Capital. He also led Martha Stewart Living Omnimedia in 2003 and 2004, during a period when lifestyle entrepreneur Martha Stewart faced federal securities and obstruction charges.The Ubbens made headlines in 2019 after donating $50 million to support scholarships at Northwestern University.Now listed for $22 million, the Healdsburg estate brings together a working vineyard, distinctive architecture, designer interiors and a connection to Hollywood history. Once part of MacMurray’s cattle ranch, the property has evolved into a private wine-country retreat with three homes, river access and established Pinot Noir vines.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: Just Eat apologises for AI food mistakes after social media ridicule
articles.summary: A spokesperson said it was removing inaccurate AI images and pausing the rollout of the tool.
articles.body:
Just Eat has apologised after it was ridiculed online over a series of mistakes with AI-generated pictures for some of its restaurants' food items.

The online food delivery platform had been testing out the tech to showcase food which didn't have images yet - but not all turned out as planned.

Instead the AI invented several bizarre concoctions, from bacon and eggs floating in a glass of cola - a confusion between "soda" and "soda bread" - to chips poking out of muffins.

A Just Eat spokesperson said the firm was "in the process of removing" the incorrect images, and would stop making more until the AI was further developed.

"We work with tens of thousands of small restaurants on their food imagery, including funding professional local photographers," the spokesperson told the BBC.

"We've been trialling AI-enhanced images, and as with any new technology, it isn't always quite right the first time."

The incident highlights the difficulties companies can still face when using AI to speed up or simplify work processes, especially when it is used to interpret words in a specific context.

Members of the Just Eat UK subreddit have flocked to the site over the past few days to post the latest unintentionally hilarious spins on takeaway food items.

Any picture generated using AI on the delivery app appears with a label indicating so, and the BBC has spotted many of the more unusual takes still up on menus.

A Belfast cafe, meanwhile, had its bacon and egg soda bread dish represented as a glass of fizzy drink with a cooked egg and bacon floating in it.

Spelling mistakes on menu items have sometimes added to the confusion, with the Instagram account @uknewestfoods posting a picture of garlic bread in the shape of a plane - presumably because of a misspelling of the word "plain".

Meanwhile, a "cheese roll" - bread and cheese - instead became slabs of cheese rolled into a sushi roll.

While some on social media said they found the images "hilarious", another was less interested in the AI-generated dishes, saying: "Well, that lot just helped my diet".

Meanwhile, one person on Instagram questioned why customers would ever want to see AI images of a restaurant's food even if they were closer to the real thing.

"I want to see what the dish actually looks like as it helps me decide who to order from or what to order," they said.

"These 'perfect' AI versions just lead to disappointment if that's what you think your meal will look like."

articles.title: 'Mindset shift' needed within government for No10 North to work, says deputy
articles.summary: Number 10 North deputy director Duncan Parish has told a conference he is still facing "institutional barriers".
articles.body:
A "mindset shift" is needed across the UK's central government to help Number 10 North deliver its objectives, its deputy director has said.

Duncan Parish told a conference in Lincolnshire on Wednesday there were "institutional challenges" within government that needed to be overcome to deliver change.

The Manchester office of Number 10 North - sister to London's Downing Street - was set up by Prime Minister Andy Burnham in July.

Burnham's political opponents have called the office a "gimmick" and raised transparency concerns about the costs involved.

Speaking to the Great Exhibition conference of local political and business leaders, Parish said his career in the civil service to date had "not been without its frustrations" and there can be "friction" between different parts of government which have "similar but ever so slightly competing objectives".

Parish, a civil servant in Whitehall before moving to Manchester four years ago, said Number 10 North staff were "delivering outcomes at a national level across a huge range of areas" including health, transport, education and social care.

"But we continually need to work to overcome those institutional challenges," he added.

He said one priority of Number 10 North was to "shift power and accountability" closer to local areas, but acknowledged "that means reforming the civil service as well" - by not viewing national, regional and local government as separate.

Describing Number 10 North's second focus of growth, Parish told local leaders: "We're here to unblock issues that may have become stalled or where boundaries within government end up being a hindrance."

He said that "too often, working within government or departments can be perceived as either difficult or slow".

"But to deliver that change, requires us all to change - and part of that change is a mindset shift within central government," he said.

"We need to focus on the whole country and work across those boundaries, bringing in mayoral strategic authorities like Greater Lincolnshire into discussions that previously they may not have been part of - working bottom-up, rather than top-down."

His comments come as the government continues to face questions about the cost to the taxpayer of the new headquarters.

In September, Conservative shadow minister Mike Wood raised concerns about "little information and so little transparency" surrounding Number 10 North which he described as a "gimmick".

"The minister either doesn't know or won't tell us how much No 10 North will cost, how many people work there or how many of them actually turn up to work - it's almost as though this hasn't been properly thought through," he told a House of Commons debate.

He called for the annual budget, staff levels and office attendance statistics to be published. Current staffing levels have also not yet been clarified.

Cabinet Office minister Sally Jameson said last week that the government did not know how much has been spent on hotels for No 10 North staff, ministers and special advisers travelling between London and Manchester since it opened.

The cost is "not centrally collated" but is "being met within existing departmental budgets", Jameson said in response to a parliamentary question.

Number 10 North's latest summit of regional mayors, held in its "situation room", will take place on Thursday. Burnham has previously indicated he will work there at least once a week, and hosted the Irish Taoiseach Micheál Martin in September .

Parish added in his speech: "How will we know if Number 10 North is working?

"Ultimately, success will be in people in the UK feeling the difference in their communities, with greater opportunities, improved living standards, faster decisions...more joined up services and a stronger voices in the future of their place."

articles.title: Andy Burnham proposes plan to cut standing charges from gas bills
articles.summary: The prime minister provided little detail, and there are questions over shifting the fees onto unit costs.
articles.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has asked ministers to develop a plan to remove standing charges from gas bills.

These are fixed daily fees that cover the costs of connecting to a supply. They vary by region and households must still pay them even when energy is not being used.

Industry body Energy UK said whether the proposed changes would make a difference to bills would depend on how or where the charges were reallocated on the bill.

But an influential research foundation argued it would be a progressive move that would help those on low-incomes and knock £27 off a typical annual bill.

During Prime Minister's Questions, Burnham said the "pragmatic decision" on giving the green light to the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea would allow the government to increase investment in renewables and "do more to help people with bills".

He said he had asked the Chancellor John Healey and Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh "to look at whether we can remove standing charges from gas bills and to report back to this house at the earliest opportunity".

No details have been given on how removing standing charges would work in practice. But the suggestion has been made by research firm Nesta that they could be moved to the unit rate , so people pay for what they use.

This would probably benefit customers who don't use much gas, but heavy users could end up paying more.

For nearly two years, regulator Ofgem has run a series of consultations on standing charges, with a massive public response including vociferous opposition from low-energy users who can do nothing to cut standing charges.

Ofgem is running a pilot scheme on low standing charge tariffs, but is yet to draw any firm conclusions, suggesting there are no easy answers.

Higher cost of electricity standing charges

Average standing charges are 54.8p a day for electricity and 29.7p a day for gas.

When asked why electricity standing charges would not be scrapped as well, the PM's official spokesman said VAT had already been cut on electricity bills.

Standing charges cover costs such as transporting energy to homes via pipes and wires, and the upkeep of that infrastructure.

The standing charges also fund schemes to support low-income households.

Many of these costs will need to be recouped somehow, but Citizens Advice has warned about the potential consequences of reform for vulnerable customers.

Vulnerable people who don't have a high income, but have high energy usage, could be penalised.

But Madeleine Gabriel, director of sustainable future at Nesta, said: "Abolishing the gas standing charge and moving those costs onto the unit rate would help those worst hit by rising energy prices."

Pressure remains on the chancellor to offer more fundamental, targeted energy support this winter in his Budget next week, with energy prices forecast to rise by 16% to a four-year high in January .

In addition to standing charges, Burnham said investing in renewables would also bring household bills down "substantially" by breaking the link between gas and electricity prices "in this parliament".

Electricity prices in the UK are mainly set by gas prices, and this is often cited as a reason why electricity prices in the UK are higher than many other countries.

articles.title: Grandfather gunned down in road rage attack days after burying Air Force son; convicted murderer charged
articles.summary: Surveillance video captures the deadly road rage confrontation that left grandfather Nelson Batista dead on a Bridgeport street after a scuffle.
articles.body: A Connecticut man who was sentenced to 30 years in prison for a 1992 felony murder conviction has been arrested again in connection with a road rage shooting that left a grandfather dead in Bridgeport, according to city police. Jorge "George" Ortiz, 57, was arrested after a brief foot chase Monday to end a week-long manhunt and charged with murder, criminal possession of a pistol and carrying a pistol without a permit, Bridgeport police said in a statement. He is accused of gunning down 48-year-old Nelson Batista, a grandfather who recently laid his 25-year-old Air Force airman son to rest, in a 9 a.m. road rage incident on Oct. 12, according to a police affidavit. PREGNANT WOMAN DRIVING HOME FROM PRENATAL VISIT SHOT DURING ALLEGED ROAD RAGE ATTACK: POLICE Ortiz and Batista were strangers, according to Bridgeport Police Chief Roderick Porter. "This was a random act," he told reporters at a news briefing announcing the arrest — just hours before Batista's funeral. Surveillance video shows a man identified as Ortiz following a woman down Park Avenue as the victim turned his SUV down a side street, according to the affidavit. Ortiz allegedly slapped his hands on the side of the car, prompting the driver to stop and get out. Ortiz allegedly punched the victim first, and they fell to the ground in a scuffle before surveillance video showed them struggling for control of a handgun, according to the affidavit. The city's ShotSpotter program captured at least two gunshots, with the medical examiner later determining one struck Batista in the chest. APPARENT ROAD RAGE DRIVER APPEARS TO THREATEN MOM ON CAMERA AS 3-YEAR-OLD CRIES IN BACK SEAT SEND US A TIP He died at the hospital. Police credited tips from the community for Ortiz's capture after a woman recorded some of the incident on cellphone video and other witnesses helped identify him. Video taken from inside a vehicle captured some of the scuffle, including the attacker getting up, striking Batista in the head with the butt of a pistol and taking off as the victim lies motionless in the street. LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST A detective recognized Ortiz from prior encounters, including one in March, according to the affidavit. He had been arrested on misdemeanor drug charges in a case that is still pending. Police also received a tip from a man who also said he could identify Ortiz as the man in the photo. Batista was an avid fan of Major League Baseball and the NFL, according to his own obituary, and especially fond of the New York Yankees. He was a father of six and grandfather of three.

articles.title: In 2017, a Massachusetts man bought an old religious drawing for just $30 at an estate sale; experts later attributed it to Renaissance master Albrecht Dürer and placed its potential value above $10 million
articles.summary: A $30 estate-sale purchase in Massachusetts has turned into one of the most remarkable art discoveries of recent years.
articles.body: A $30 estate-sale purchase in Massachusetts has turned into one of the most remarkable art discoveries of recent years. The small, unframed drawing, bought by an anonymous man in 2017, has been identified by leading scholars as an original work by German Renaissance master Albrecht Dürer. Now titled 'The Virgin and Child With a Flower on a Grassy Bench' and dated to 1503, the ink sketch is believed to be worth at least $10 million, with some estimates placing its value far higher. The news was reported by NPR, Smithsonian Magazine and Artnet News. Read more about it here:A bargain no one expectedThe buyer came across the drawing at an estate sale in Massachusetts, where it was displayed without a frame and priced at just $30. It showed a mother and child rendered in delicate ink on yellowed linen, and although it carried Dürer’s well-known “A.D.” monogram, neither the seller nor the buyer believed it was a genuine Renaissance work.The anonymous purchaser later said he bought it simply because he thought it was “a wonderfully rendered piece of old art,” as per the reports. He kept it at home, unaware that the modest sheet of paper might be an original drawing by one of the most important artists of the Northern Renaissance.The work had been sold by the daughters of the late architect Jean-Paul Carlhian. Their family had long assumed it was a modern reproduction, though its history appears to reach back to 19th-century French art collectors among the Carlhian ancestors.From curiosity to masterpieceAccording to Smithsonian Magazine, the turning point came in 2019, when art collector and Agnews Gallery shareholder Clifford Schorer heard rumours about the possible Dürer during a trip to Boston. After seeing the drawing, he described the moment as extraordinary, saying it was either the greatest forgery he had ever seen or a masterpiece.Experts then spent years examining the work. Their investigation focused on the materials, the monogram, the paper and the drawing’s relationship to Dürer’s known compositions. The verification process ultimately took about three years before scholars became confident that the sketch was authentic.Two details proved especially persuasive. First, Dürer had inscribed his initials using the same ink as the drawing itself, a practice seen on at least 20 other works made between 1501 and 1514. Second, paper conservator Jane McAusland identified a trident and ring watermark on the sheet, a motif found on more than 200 sheets known to have been used by the artist.Scholars confirm the attributionLeading Dürer specialists Christof Metzger, head curator at Vienna’s Albertina Museum, and Giulia Bartrum, formerly a curator at the British Museum, examined the drawing and judged it authentic, reports shared. Their assessment transformed what had been treated as an attractive old sketch into a newly recognised work by a Renaissance master.The drawing is now dated to 1503 and titled The Virgin and Child With a Flower on a Grassy Bench. Scholars believe Dürer created it as a preparatory study for 'The Virgin Among a Multitude of Animals', a separate composition held by the Albertina Museum in Vienna.The image depicts the Virgin Mary seated with the Christ child on a grassy bench beside a simple wooden fence. Dürer gave the scene an unusually lively quality by showing Jesus as a squirming toddler rather than a calm infant, twisting away from the viewer and turning his attention toward his mother.Why it could be worth millionsWhen the discovery became public in 2022, NPR reported that the drawing was believed to be worth around $10 million. Smithsonian Magazine later noted that experts suggested it could be worth upward of $50 million, reflecting both Dürer’s stature and the rarity of a previously unknown work by the artist.The drawing was exhibited at Agnews Gallery in London, with plans for an eventual sale. Because Dürer works rarely appear on the market, and because this was the first completely unknown drawing by the artist to resurface since the 1970s, interest from major institutions and private collectors was expected to be intense.For the anonymous buyer, the discovery turned a casual $30 purchase into an extraordinary windfall. For the art world, it was a reminder that important works can survive unnoticed in attics, family collections and estate sales, waiting for someone with the knowledge to recognise them.A lesson in looking closelyThe story resonates because it combines luck, curiosity and expertise. The buyer did not set out to find a Dürer, but he recognised that the drawing had artistic quality and was worth investigating further. That instinct led to a process that connected a small sheet of paper to one of Europe’s greatest Renaissance artists.It also highlights the importance of provenance, materials and scholarly review. A signature alone is not enough to establish authenticity, but the matching ink, historic watermark and expert analysis together built a compelling case that this was no reproduction.More than five centuries after Dürer made the drawing, a $30 estate-sale find became a multimillion-dollar Renaissance treasure. It is a striking example of how art history can still surprise us, sometimes in the most ordinary places.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.summary: Almudena Garcia describes the terrifying moment a mob of rioters turned on her husband in central Paris, leaving him bloodied.
articles.body: A woman who watched her husband get brutally beaten by a mob of rioters in Paris is recounting the terrifying attack that left him bloodied. "It was like a horror movie. I've never experienced a fear like that before," Almudena Garcia told "America's Newsroom" on Wednesday. "We were just in the streets in the center of Paris ... We were about to leave, and then we heard some screaming, so we turned around, and we saw one of our friends being beat up by a group of individuals, four or five, and then my husband just ran to them in order to help his friends," she added. MCDONALD'S RANSACKED AND WRECKED AS STORES, RESTAURANTS SUFFER FROM VIOLENCE AND RIOTING Garcia, who lives in France, told Fox News the group turned on her husband and began beating him after he tried to help his friend. "It happened very, very fast," she recounted. "There were five at the beginning and four or five more just arrived in two seconds, so I just saw my husband being beat up by 10 individuals." Garcia said she screamed for help during the attack, fearing her husband could be seriously injured or killed. "I was panicking, and I was asking for help," she said. According to Garcia, two waiters at a nearby restaurant intervened and pulled her husband inside to protect him from the attackers. She said several members of the group then followed him into the restaurant and continued the assault. FRANCE'S MASSIVE INTEL FAILURE SPARKS RESIGNATION OFFERS AMID DAYS OF RIOTING "Thanks to the waiters, they could finally get them [the rioters] out ... and I got into the restaurant, and I just saw my husband all covered in blood ... It was very, very scary," she added. The attack comes amid weeks of unrest across France, which began over concerns about poor school conditions, has expanded to include protests against rising living costs. Some demonstrations have turned violent, with rioters attacking police, looting businesses and damaging public buildings. Paris has remained a flash point for violence, with videos circulating on social media over the weekend appearing to show groups of men damaging property in the capital and other major cities. Violence in the streets has subsided since French authorities imposed curfews in parts of Paris and other cities affected by the unrest, according to The Associated Press. Authorities are preparing for additional demonstrations on Saturday, Oct. 24. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Fox News' Robert Schmad contributed to this report.

articles.title: Bush family members back Democrat James Talarico in Texas Senate race
articles.summary: The Bushes could potentially influence some disaffected Republicans when it comes to next month's vote.
articles.body:
Two members of the Bush family, the Republican political dynasty that counts Texas as its political launchpad, have backed Democrat James Talarico in the hotly fought race for a Senate seat in the Lone Star State.

Barbara Bush, daughter of ex-President George W Bush, has reportedly donated to Talarico's campaign, while her uncle, Neil Bush, says he backs the Democrat.

The Republican candidate, Ken Paxton, beat a primary challenge from Neil Bush's nephew, so the endorsement may be cast by critics as political sour grapes.

But the Bushes could potentially influence some disaffected Republican voters when it comes to next month's vote. No Democrat has won a Texas Senate seat since 1988.

Opinion polls show Paxton and Talarico neck and neck ahead of the 3 November midterm elections, which will decide which party controls Congress.

Neil Bush said he was opposing Paxton because of his efforts to help President Donald Trump deny his 2020 election loss to Joe Biden.

In a post on Facebook late on Tuesday, Neil Bush wrote that he had cast his ballot for Talarico as early voting began.

"My vote was motivated by two things: deep concern about Ken Paxton's record and genuine admiration for the character and principles I see in James Talarico," Neil Bush wrote on Facebook.

A businessman who has never held political office, Neil Bush is remembered for his role as director of the Silverado Savings and Loan when it collapsed in 1988, costing taxpayers more than $1bn.

Meanwhile, Barbara Bush has donated to help Talarico, campaign finance records show.

Bush, the twin of US chat show host Jenna Hager Bush, reportedly gave $2,500 (£1,900) to a political action committee that supports the Democrat.

The BBC has contacted Barbara Bush for comment.

A survivor of several political scandals, Paxton was previously impeached by fellow Republicans in the Texas state legislature.

He also beat a primary challenge from the son of Jeb Bush, George P Bush.

The Bushes have had a complex relationship with Trump since he beat Jeb Bush, the former Florida governor, during the 2016 Republican presidential primary race.

Former President George HW Bush previously called Trump a "blow hard" and confirmed he had voted for Democrat Hillary Clinton in the 2016 race.

His son, George W Bush, whom Trump repeatedly lambasted for launching the US war in Iraq, has made thinly veiled criticisms of Trump.

But during his own political campaigns, George P Bush backed Trump.

articles.title: This is why your nose gets raw when you’re sick, and here’s how to prevent it, according to doctors
articles.summary: Ear, nose and throat doctors explain why your nose gets raw and irritated during a cold, how to prevent it and the products that can soothe your nostrils and septum.
articles.body: Fewer things make cold season more miserable than a nose that’s red, raw and sore. Between dry indoor heat, chilly outdoor air and constant nose blowing, the delicate skin around your nostrils and the inside of your nose, including the septum, can quickly become dry, cracked and irritated. For some people that means flaking and tenderness. For others it means painful sores or even nosebleeds. To find out why this happens and what you can do about it, I spoke with two ear, nose and throat doctors (ENTs). Below, they explain what causes nasal irritation during colder months, the simple habits that can help prevent it and the products for soothing and healing your nose if irritation has already set in, especially when you’re sick. The best products to soothe irritation inside your nose I rounded up products that can help soothe existing irritation or prevent it from starting, both inside and around the nose. All of them fall into product categories the ENT doctors I spoke with recommended, so you can feel confident adding them to your cold-season routine. Vaseline’s fragrance-free, hypoallergenic jelly forms a protective barrier that seals in moisture, making it an easy fix for skin rubbed raw by constant nose blowing. “For the skin around the nose and philtrum (the indented area between your nose and top lip), a simple moisturizer or protective ointment can help,” says Dr. Madeleine Herman, an ENT physician and president of the Sinus Center and ENT Specialists of Houston. One tub should last you all season. “Nasal emollient sprays can provide much-needed moisture to the nasal cavity during a cold,” says Dr. Ryan Salvador, an ENT surgeon at Sinus and Snoring Specialists in Austin —he recommends this emollient. It contains a blend of botanical oils, including pine, eucalyptus, peppermint and cottonseed, that moisturizes dry, inflamed nasal passages. It comes with a dropper, so you can apply it directly inside your nostrils where irritation tends to start. Fair warning: It has a strong, menthol-like scent. Unlike thicker ointments, this water-based saline gel is designed to go inside your nostrils as well as around them, making it a handy pick if the irritation is on your septum. Its formula combines saline and aloe to moisturize dry nasal passages and calm tenderness from colds, allergies and winter air. The brand recommends applying it during the day and at bedtime to prevent drying and crusting, and the small tube easily fits in a pocket or bag. This saline spray blends propolis, eucalyptus, oregano oil and xylitol to clear congestion while moisturizing irritated nasal passages. “Using nasal saline to clean the nose is very helpful,” says Salvador. “They usually come in two concentrations — 0.9 percent and three percent. The former can moisturize the nose and thin excess mucus. The latter can cause decongestion, but tends to have mild irritation.” This one falls into the former category and shoppers say they love how easy it is to use the point-and-pump bottle. “Gentle nose-blowing with soft and fragrance-free tissues can also help clear excess mucus,” says Salvador. “This helps to reduce nasal drainage, which can irritate the skin outside the nose.” These tissues are thick, three-ply and fragrance-free, so they’re gentle enough for a nose that’s already raw from constant blowing. They’re also sturdy enough to hold up to a big sneeze without tearing. This cool mist humidifier can help keep your nose hydrated as you sleep. It is designed to automatically shut off when the device detects it has run out of water and the essential oil tray also lets the machine double as a diffuser to add a pleasant scent throughout your home. Also nice: It is slim and tall, which means it doesn’t take up too much surface area on a counter or side table. Why does the inside of your nose get irritated when you have a cold? Catching a cold doesn’t just leave you congested. It can set off a chain reaction inside your nose that can leave the tissue there swollen, tender and raw. Much of that discomfort comes from your body’s own defenses working overtime. “During a cold, any of the 200 viruses that can cause such an infection enter the nose. This results in the white blood cells in the area causing swelling and inflammation to the nasal tissues,” says Salvador. “These then release specific cell messengers that dilate blood vessels (so more immune cells can reach the infected site) and increase mucus production (to trap virus particles). However, the swelling and mucus production can cause the nasal tissues to feel irritated.” All that extra mucus creates a second problem: constant wiping and blowing. “When you create more snot or mucus, it causes you to blow, wipe, rub the nose more, which can irritate the delicate skin and lining of the nose, including the septum,” says Herman. “Then, dry indoor air can make the problem even worse.” How can you stop the inside of your nose from getting irritated when you have a cold? The good news is that a few small habits can go a long way toward keeping your nose comfortable while you recover. “The best way to avoid an irritated nose is moisture and treating your delicate nasal tissue with care,” says Herman. “Try gently blowing your nose, rather than repeatedly wiping or aggressively blowing. Saline nasal spray can help keep the nasal lining moist and loosen mucus so you don’t have to work as hard to clear your nose.” Adding moisture to your environment, and to your body, helps too. “A humidifier, especially while you sleep, and keeping yourself hydrated can also help,” says Herman. Running one overnight can counteract the dry indoor heat that tends to make irritation worse during colder months. Want more from NBC Selected? articles.title: In 2022, Kippen architects at Paper Igloo won a RIAS Award for Ostro Passivhaus, the hand-built home they worked on over eight years of evenings and weekends
articles.summary: Discover the award-winning Ostro Passivhaus in Kippen, Scotland, built by architects Paper Igloo. Explore its eco-friendly design, stunning features, and construction journey that took eight years to complete.
articles.body: Kippen is a conservation village in Stirlingshire, Scotland, a short drive from Stirling. Its streets are lined with older stone houses, and new buildings there are closely watched. A modern timber house on a plot behind existing homes has to fit in without copying its neighbors. Passivhaus is a voluntary building standard that emphasizes low energy consumption through heavy insulation and airtightness with controlled ventilation. The certification is given after an independent verification of both the design and the completed building. It is uncommon for architects to build their own Passivhaus home for their family, let alone do the work themselves.Starting a self-build in Kippen in March 2014 and certification in October 2017Architect Mhairi Grant and her partner Martin McCrae, who run Paper Igloo Ltd, began the project in March 2014, the Passivhaus Trust’s project page says. The timber-frame house has a treated floor area of 170 m², cost £250,000 and was designed for three occupants. It records airtightness of 0.2 ACH@50Pa and a thermal energy demand of 15 kWh/m²/yr, and the owners said the compact services and painstaking attention to detail helped deliver that performance. RIBA’s awards entry describes the house as an eight-year labor of love built by the architect-owners in evenings and weekends, with their practice acting as principal contractor. According to the practice page at RIAS, the house was completed in 2020. This could mean that the eight years also involved design, planning, construction, and completion.Four summers of cladding and a house named for an Adriatic windThe RIBA award entry says the owners spent four summers cutting and installing the exterior cladding, one summer for each side of the house. The house sits in the Kippen conservation area on a backland site reached by a shared driveway. Grand Designs Magazine says the name Ostro comes from the southerly wind in the Adriatic. It describes a south-facing, double-height house clad in Siberian larch and built as a timber “box in a box” with a continuous thermal break of wood fiber insulation. A central two-story black timber cube holds the service spaces. The magazine says the cube recalls the entrance to Charles Rennie Mackintosh’s Hill House. It includes drawers built into the stairs and a gin store beside the kitchen worktop.Embodied carbon, contract value and sizeOstro Passivhaus was a joint winner in the Residential New Build category at the 2023 UK Passivhaus Awards, according to Paper Igloo’s project page. The practice’s recognition page also lists a commendation at the 2021 Saltire Society Housing Design Awards and wins in the Best Green Home and Home of the Future categories at the 2021 Daily Telegraph Homebuilding & Renovating Awards. The page claims that it complies with the Gold standard of section 7 (Sustainability) of Scottish Technical Standards.The RIAS practice page lists a contract value of £250,000, which is a recorded figure and not necessarily the final total cost of the self-build. It lists the size as a 132 square metre footprint and gives 2020 as the completion year. In its award announcement, the Royal Incorporation of Architects in Scotland said the owners built the house by hand over several years on a modest budget.The June 2022 RIAS Award and the prizes that followedIn June 2022, RIAS announced eight winners of its national architecture awards, and Ostro Passivhaus was one of them. The judges described it as an exemplary low-energy home that disproves the idea that fine contemporary architecture cannot also be environmentally beneficial. They added that nothing in it is unnecessary and that every part contributes to the building’s story. Paper Igloo also won the RIAS Circular Economy Design Award, sponsored by Zero Waste Scotland, in the same month. Its practice page lists further 2022 results, including the Scottish Design Awards Chairman’s Award in architecture, the residential prize from the same awards, and an honorable mention in the ASBP Awards.Paper Igloo’s official project page confirms that Ostro Passivhaus was a joint winner in the Residential New Build category at the 2023 UK Passivhaus Awards. articles.title: Helen Haines: 'Targeted' attack on much-loved Australian MP leaves Wangaratta heartbroken
articles.summary: Locals describe the MP, who had to have both legs amputated, as a genuinely kind person who fought for the community.
articles.body:
Wangaratta has been thrust into an unwelcome spotlight this week. Residents in this rural Victorian town are used to catering to tourists passing through on their way to regional wineries, or music lovers visiting its annual jazz and blues festival.

Instead, locals are fielding endless questions about their MP - and having to explain to strangers what it all means for the town's nearly 30,000 people.

They are clearly in shock about what police say was a targeted and deliberate attack on Helen Haines on Monday afternoon, when she was struck by a car just outside her office.

"People are simply dumbfounded and finding it very hard to fathom the scale of this tragedy," Australia's Governor-General Sam Mostyn, who represents King Charles, said at a press conference on Wednesday.

The independent federal MP had to have both legs amputated after she was airlifted to Melbourne. But the "two most important parts of Helen", her heart and her mind, were in "good shape", her husband Phil Haines said.

The MP isn't a divisive figure, locals tell the BBC, and no one can understand why she was allegedly targeted.

"Everyone knows Helen," says Jane Hill, who owns a party supply shop a few hundred metres down the town's main street from where Haines was hit.

"She is a such a good person in our community. She'd go to everything - celebrations, funerals, she's one of those genuinely kind people - and so are her family."

Local man Brendan Nugent, whose father has been good friends with Haines for decades, faces at least three charges over the alleged attack including intentionally causing harm and appeared in court on Wednesday. Police say they are considering further charges, including attempted murder.

MP 'thanked everyone' as she lay injured

First elected to parliament in 2019, Haines is best known for her years-long efforts to establish a national anti-corruption commission.

She was spurred by on a series of major political scandals which, in her words, saw "public money spent for political gain", disproportionate spending on "shiny infrastructure projects" in marginal seats and decisions benefitting big donors over ordinary people.

The commission finally opened in 2023 under Anthony Albanese's Labor government.

Haines has also helped to secure funds for housebuilding, railway improvements and health infrastructure in her region, which she argues has long been sidelined by policies favouring cities.

On a spring afternoon in Wangaratta, nobody seemed to have a bad word to say about the former nurse and midwife turned politician.

Local Mayor Irene Grant described her as "warm", "cheerful" and "committed", and pointed to her record on climate action and Indigenous rights.

In a police update on Wednesday, Victoria Police Commissioner Mike Bush said she'd given "wonderful support" to local police when two officers were shot dead in the nearby town of Porepunkah last year.

Bystanders who came to Haines' aid recalled how she thanked them even as she lay severely injured.

"It was incredible," Jacklyn Black told Nine Network's Today show. "We were having conversations, she was telling me about her grandkids."

"To be in that situation and be as calm as she could be in the moment, but also thankful to the aid that the community had given her... I could [not] speak any more highly of her in a moment like that," Cody Lepoidevin added.

There's a large print-out of Helen Haines plastered onto the window of her office - anyone delivering flowers for her gets a big smile back as they look up and walk away.

Across the road on Tuesday, a man waved an Australian flag. On his T-shirt were the words "Wangaratta - this is not us!!"

It's clear that many feel that way in this friendly community where people look out for each other.

Next door to Haines' office is RickyChops barbershop, owned by Ricky Jefferies. When he heard the chaos unfolding outside, he rushed to help , pinning down the suspect.

"I just leant over him and once he was on the ground and he was no longer a threat, I just stood with him, and I told him that he can't leave," he explained after the incident.

"I don't think I'm a hero. I think that I just was a person who had an opportunity to intervene in a safe-ish sort of way."

Some clearly disagree with Ricky. By Tuesday afternoon, he too had received a bouquet of flowers tied to his shop's door, and a small balloon with the words "thank you".

Down the road at the Holy Trinity Anglican Cathedral, a vigil was held, attended by a couple of hundred people lining up to light a candle for Haines.

Some hugged the clergy, while others wore campaign T-shirts carrying the words "Team Helen Haines".

Her husband Phil said he had received "thousands upon thousands" of messages of love and support.

"I can only say how much of a difference that makes to all of us," he said. "Helen's road to recovery will be long and difficult, but we know she is a fighter."

"Whether you vote for her or not, she seems to have the community at heart so that's all you can really ask for; a politician that represents your community," said Austin Longfield who lives in nearby Albury.

"It's just something that you wouldn't expect in our community," he added. "You see it in other countries and it's just something that I didn't comprehend could happen here."

articles.title: CJP protest: India 'cockroach' leaders who called on election chief to quit are freed from jail
articles.summary: Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka were accused of breaking into an unauthorised protest venue in Delhi.
articles.body:
Two leaders of the Gen Z-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) have been freed from jail a week after they were arrested for trespassing at a banned protest site in Delhi.

Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka walked out of Tihar jail hours after a magistrate ordered their release. They had been detained by police and jailed after they crossed barricades and climbed over the locked gate at Jantar Mantar.

The historic venue was recently removed from a list of designated protest sites.

The men, who denied wrongdoing, have been calling on India's chief election commissioner to resign. Critics accuse the commission of manipulating voter rolls to benefit India's governing party, charges the commission rejects.

A special executive magistrate court in Delhi, passed their release order, legal news website Bar and Bench reported.

After bail was granted, Das told reporters from a police van: "Truth alone triumphs. Long live the revolution."

Das and Ranka are key leaders of the CJP, which began as an internet joke in May after India's top judge compared unemployed young people to "cockroaches".

The CJP is not a registered political party, but a collective which began by mobilising thousands of young people to protest over leaked exam papers.

By July it had emerged as a major force.

A march towards parliament that month ended in clashes with police, drawing wider attention to the movement and increasing pressure on the government. The unrest eventually led to the resignation of India's education minister .

The CJP has since shifted its focus to India's electoral system.

Along with opposition parties, students and other critics of the government, it accuses Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar of revising electoral rolls, an exercise known as the Special Intensive Revision (SIR), to benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi's governing Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).

Both the BJP and the Election Commission have rejected the allegation.

The SIR exercise has resulted in around 130 million names being removed from voter lists since last year.

Critics warn that the process could also exclude eligible voters, potentially denying them their right to vote, while the Election Commission says the exercise is intended to remove ineligible, dead and duplicate entries.
