articles.title: In 1902, Pennsylvania began buying nearly treeless, fire-damaged land for just 18 cents to $2 an acre; decades of replanting added more than a million trees and helped build Promised Land State Park
articles.summary: Promised Land State Park in Pennsylvania is now a forested retreat of lakes, trails and campgrounds, but little more than a century ago the land was
articles.body: Promised Land State Park in Pennsylvania is now a forested retreat of lakes, trails and campgrounds, but little more than a century ago the land was almost bare. Between 1902 and 1904, the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania bought the fire-damaged, heavily logged property for between 18 cents and $2 per acre. Decades of replanting followed, including more than a million trees planted by the Civilian Conservation Corps, transforming a scarred landscape into one of the state’s most beloved parks. Read more about its history, as documented by the Pennsylvania Department of Conservation and Natural Resources:Land shaped by loggingLong before it became a state park, the land was home to the Minsi Tribe of the Wolf Clan of the Lenni Lenape. In the 19th century, the area passed through private ownership and became part of extensive timber holdings, including land acquired by Dr Joseph Jones in 1869.Early European settlers and lumber operators built sawmills to process the area’s large stands of conifer and hardwood trees. The forests were repeatedly clear-cut, and by 1903 the land was almost completely without trees. The loss of forest brought serious consequences. Erosion increased, wildfires became more damaging and wildlife lost the habitat it needed to survive. What had once been a thriving woodland had become a damaged, nearly treeless landscape.Pennsylvania buys the landAs per the website, Pennsylvania began purchasing the land from 1902 to 1904, paying between 18 cents and $2 per acre. In 1905, Promised Land became the fourth state park in Pennsylvania, marking the beginning of a long recovery effort. The state did not simply preserve the land as it found it. It began restoring the forest, planting trees across the damaged terrain and creating facilities that would allow people to experience the outdoors. Between 1902 and 1933, the Commonwealth planted more than 370,000 trees.Public recreation developed alongside the reforestation work. The first campground was established in 1905 in a pine plantation between Bear Wallow Road and the stream flowing into Lower Lake. It closed in 1925 and was replaced by a new campground in what is now the main beach picnic area.The CCC transforms the parkThe most dramatic phase of restoration came during the Great Depression. In 1933, President Franklin D Roosevelt created the Civilian Conservation Corps, a programme that gave young unemployed men food, clothing and a small wage in exchange for conservation work. Promised Land’s Camp S-139-PA opened in May 1933 and operated until July 1941. It was located in what are now the Deerfield and Pickerel Point campgrounds, and its members transformed both the park and the surrounding land. The CCC workers planted more than one million trees, fought forest fires and built roads, trails and recreational facilities. Their work included Pickerel Point campground, the Bear Wallow cabins, much of North Shore Road and the Egypt Meadow Dam.A park built by restorationToday, Promised Land State Park reflects the combined effort of early state reforestation and CCC labour. The once-barren land now supports forests, wildlife and outdoor recreation, making it difficult to imagine how bare and fire-damaged the property was in the early 1900s.The park’s history also shows how conservation can repair damage caused by unsustainable logging. Rather than abandoning the land, Pennsylvania invested in it, replanted it and gradually rebuilt an ecosystem that could support both nature and public enjoyment. Each August, the park celebrates the CCC legacy with a festival. It is a reminder that the trails, campgrounds and forest views visitors enjoy today were shaped by generations of restoration work.Nature tests the recoveryThe park’s recovery has not been without setbacks. On May 31, 1998, an F2 tornado with winds of 113 to 157 mph cut a northeasterly path through the park, crossing Lower Lake Road, PA 390 and North Shore Road near Sucker Brook.More than 500 people were trapped in the park overnight, but no one was seriously injured. The event became part of the park’s modern history and is remembered in the booklet After the Wind Died Down, held by the park office.Promised Land State Park remains a powerful example of what long-term conservation can achieve. From land bought for as little as 18 cents an acre to a forest restored with more than a million trees, its story is one of recovery, public investment and the enduring value of protecting natural landscapes.You use AI every day. articles.title: Fuel leak which killed fish in River Taff stopped
articles.summary: GE Aerospace previously confirmed fuel got into the river while repair work took place nearby.
articles.body:
A fuel leak in the River Taff which killed fish and sparked a warning for people to shut their windows has now stopped, official have said.

Officers from Natural Resources Wales (NRW) on Wedneaday the source of the pollution affecting the Taff in places such as Nantgarw, Treforest and Taffs Well since 16 October over.

GE Aerospace previously confirmed fuel got into the river while repair work took place at its site nearby, but NRW said it was working to determine how fuel entered the drainage system and reached the river.

NRW added it had found fewer than 10 dead fish and impacts to aquatic invertebrates as a result of the leak.

NRW said the source was identified at 19:30 BST on Friday, after kerosene spread down almost 2.5 miles (4km) of the river.

It added evidence was being compiled and reviewed as part of the ongoing investigation.

The environmental body also received reports of pollution affecting the Taff in Glan Y Llyn, Gwaelod-y-garth and Tongwynlais.

In an update on Sunday evening, NRW said due to the nature of the incident, identifying how the fuel entered the drainage system was difficult as it involved underground systems.

Specialist drainage and containment contractors had been sent to the site and were removing the fuel.

Eurig Thomas, a resident in Nantgarw, Rhondda Cyon Taff, told the BBC on Sunday: "It smelt like a petrol station, it hit you as soon as you came out."

Public Health Wales advised people living nearby to keep windows and doors closed, avoid any contact with the water and to call NHS 111 if they felt unwell.

articles.title: In 2001, LEGO released just 30 gold Kanohi Hau masks; 23 years later, Pennsylvania Goodwill staff found one in jewellery and sold the Bionicle rarity for $18,101
articles.summary: A rare 14-karat gold Kanohi Hau mask from LEGO's Bionicle line has sold for $18,101 after being discovered in a jewelry donation at a Pennsylvania Goodwill, highlighting its collectible value and supporting community programs.
articles.body: A small gold toy mask was tucked inside a collection of jewellery that was once donated. The item turned out to be an exceptionally rare collectable, selling for $18,101 at an online auction in February 2024. The item was a 14-karat gold Kanohi Hau mask from LEGO’s Bionicle toy line, one of just 30 gold versions reportedly produced in 2001. Initially, the staff associated with Goodwill Industries of North Central Pennsylvania listed the piece on its online auction platform for $14.95 before collectors’ interest revealed its potential value. As reported by Smithsonian Magazine on March 8, 2024, the sale turned an unassuming donation into a significant fundraising opportunity for the nonprofit organisation.A rare discovery inside a jewellery donationThe mask was donated at a Goodwill store located in State College, Pennsylvania and was part of a collection of jewellery. The mask was later sent to the company’s auction in DuBois along with other objects. In DuBois, the people who worked there examined the object. Goodwill Industries of North Central Pennsylvania’s public relations and social media coordinator, Jessica Illuzzi, told WPSU that the manager overseeing the online auction initially listed the mask for $14.95. Its significance was not immediately apparent.Interest grew when potential buyers began contacting the company about the item. Contemporary news reports suggest that some prospective buyers offered substantially more than the initial listing price, prompting staff to investigate the mask further. The piece was confirmed to be made of 14-karat gold and identified as a rare Bionicle Kanohi Hau mask. Following this, instead of selling it at the initial price, Goodwill placed it in an online auction where collectors could compete for it.Why the gold Kanohi Hau mask was so rareThis mask was part of the Bionicle collection, a construction toy. The figure toy range was released by LEGO in 2001. Due to its movable figures, unique masks, and fictional characters, the toy became quite popular among LEGO enthusiasts. In the Bionicle world, the figures wore the Kanohi masks that endowed them with certain abilities. The Hau mask signified protection, while the golden one was a collector's item.There are various accounts of how LEGO distributed these 30 Kanohi Hau masks. Most accounts point out that some of them were given away to LEGO employees while others were awarded in a promotional contest. According to a WPSU report, 25 of these were given to LEGO employees, and the remaining five were awarded in a magazine promotional contest. Even though there may be other accounts of how these 30 masks were distributed, this is the key number when it comes to the rarity of these masks.The attraction of the gold mask was in the combination of the materials used, the rarity of the mask, and the fact that it belonged to a recognisable toy line. The majority of Bionicle masks were made of plastic, while this particular mask was made of gold. Thus, the value of the mask for collectors was not limited to its role as a toy accessory.From an unpaid $33,000 bid to an $18,101 saleThe auction had an unusual complication. An earlier round of bidding was said to have gone up to $33,000, but the buyer failed to make the payment. This led to the mask being resold, and the new auction received 48 bids and ended on February 21, 2024, at $18,101. This price was still an amazing outcome for an item listed for less than $15.Following the close of the sale, Goodwill managed to utilise the proceeds of the auction for the benefit of its community budgets, financing regional employment readiness training and localised educational programs in 2024 and 2025. In this way, the sale became linked with the overall community mission of the organisation through an unusual collectable. Instead of being a stroke of luck related to a rare toy, the auction raised funds that could be used for the benefit of people seeking employment.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: A Mississippi couple received $13,172 from State Farm after a tree fell on their home, but lost their fight for a $95,896 insurance payout after an appeals court rejected their expert evidence
articles.summary: A fallen tree can leave a homeowner facing more than a damaged roof.
articles.body: A fallen tree can leave a homeowner facing more than a damaged roof. Repairs may extend to surrounding concrete, a swimming pool and parts of a building that were already showing signs of wear. For Dustin and Amanda Cain of Mississippi, the disagreement over what their insurer should cover became a legal dispute that ended with an appeals court ruling in favour of State Farm. The couple argued that the tree had caused substantially more damage than the insurer initially accepted. But their attempt to establish the full extent of the loss ran into a problem with the expert evidence they presented. On October 16, 2026, the US Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit upheld the dismissal of their claims.State Farm homeowners’ insurance dispute over tree damage and repair costsThe US Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit reported that the incident occurred on August 27, 2022, when a tree fell on the Cains’ home. The couple held a homeowners’ insurance policy with State Farm, which inspected the property and concluded that the impact had punctured the roof. The insurer attributed other problems around the house to longer-term issues, including temperature-related expansion and contraction, deferred maintenance and settlement.Those distinctions mattered because State Farm did not consider the additional damage to be covered by the policy. It initially paid the Cains $10,042.90.The couple disputed the insurer’s assessment and sought independent advice. Reportedly, an engineer’s report and a contractor’s estimate put the cost of the damage to their home, swimming pool and concrete at $95,896.07. The figure was far above the amount State Farm had paid, setting up a disagreement over both the cause of the damage and the repairs the insurer was obliged to fund.State Farm reviewed the earlier inspection, examined the property again and revised its estimate. It then paid a further $3,130.08.Expert report raised questions about who was responsible for its findingsOn June 6, 2024, the Cains filed a lawsuit against State Farm. They sought $134,994.54, covering their breach-of-contract allegations and claims involving the insurer’s handling of the matter, along with consequential damages, legal fees, court costs and interest.Their case depended in part on demonstrating that the tree had caused the disputed damage. To support that argument, they designated Sean Fee of Forensic Building Science (FBS) as their expert witness. Fee’s report, submitted on 6 December 2024, recommended repairs but did not include a breakdown of their costs.There was a problem with the way the report had been prepared. Fee had worked on it with Jim Irmiter, a colleague at the same company, and the document stated that both men had contributed to, reviewed and agreed with its contents. Yet the Cains had formally named Fee alone as their expert.The expert evidence dispute ended with a victory for State FarmThe Cains later submitted another document, this time setting out repair costs of $149,325.66. The estimate was also jointly prepared by Fee and Irmiter, and it was filed on March 4, 2025, the deadline for completing discovery.State Farm challenged the additional estimate as well as Fee’s proposed testimony. Its position was that Fee could not simply present another person’s analysis as his own, particularly when Irmiter had not been designated as an expert witness. The insurer argued that the reports did not establish which conclusions Fee had personally reached or how he had arrived at them.The couple asked the district court to accept the later estimate despite its timing. Their lawyers explained that counsel had experienced a medical condition requiring surgeries and treatment between December 2024 and March 2025.That request did not resolve the separate issue surrounding the expert evidence. The US Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit reported that on July 24, 2025, the district court struck the proposed reports and Fee’s testimony. It found that the documents did not make clear who had performed the relevant work or developed the opinions. Without that distinction, the court concluded, the reliability of the analysis could not be properly assessed.The ruling left the Cains without the expert evidence they needed to support their account of the damage. The district court consequently granted summary judgment to State Farm and dismissed the lawsuit with prejudice, meaning the claims could not simply be brought again as a new case.The Fifth Circuit upheld the exclusion of the jointly prepared reportsThe Cains challenged the decision before the Fifth Circuit, arguing that a report did not become inadmissible merely because two people had worked on it. They maintained that Fee and Irmiter had both contributed to the documents and agreed with their conclusions, presenting a shared assessment rather than competing opinions.The appeals court did not rule that experts were prohibited from preparing reports together. Instead, it focused on the need to identify the work and opinions attributable to each person. A jointly prepared report may be acceptable, but the court must be able to determine what each designated expert actually intends to say and the reasoning supporting that testimony.In the Cains’ case, the report did not provide the necessary separation. Both Fee and Irmiter were named as contributors, but only Fee had been designated as an expert. The court therefore had no clear way to establish which parts of the analysis belonged to him.The Fifth Circuit upheld the ruling in State Farm’s favourThe Cains also argued that certain claims should survive independently, including allegations concerning delayed payment, punitive damages and actual cash value. The court rejected that position. Under Mississippi law, a bad-faith insurance claim requires an underlying breach of contract. Once the couple could no longer establish the necessary basis for their contract claim, their related allegations could not proceed on their own.The Fifth Circuit accordingly affirmed the district court’s judgment for State Farm. It did not need to decide whether the later estimate had been properly excluded as untimely or whether Fee’s proposed testimony would also have failed a separate assessment of scientific or technical reliability.The decision, issued on October 16, 2026, was marked as unpublished, meaning it was not designated for publication under the Fifth Circuit’s rules. For the Cains, the outcome was not a finding that every disputed condition at the property had been caused by long-term wear or maintenance problems. The appeal turned on whether the evidence they presented could be admitted and used to prove their case. With the expert reports excluded and no adequate alternative evidence of causation and damages, the insurer’s victory remained intact.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Bibas family relative takes fight to ICC after mother, two young boys murdered by Hamas
articles.summary: A relative of murdered mother Shiri Bibas and her sons Kfir and Ariel is pressing the ICC to act against Iranian leaders after the family’s devastating losses in the Oct. 7 attacks.
articles.body: The International Criminal Court has so far turned a blind eye to the family of Shiri Bibas and her young sons, who were brutally murdered by Iran-backed Hamas terrorists after being forcefully taken from their homes during the Oct. 7 attack on Israel. The Bibas boys — Ariel, four, Kfir, nine months, and their mother, Shiri — became the faces of the Israeli hostages held by terrorists in Gaza. All three were brutally murdered and now the mother's uncle, Maurice Shnaider, wants justice. Before the court's Chief Prosecutor, Karim Khan, was removed for misconduct, Khan oversaw the issuance of controversial arrest warrants in 2024 for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, former Israeli Defense Minister Yoav Gallant, and Hamas terror commander Mohammad Deif, alleging they had committed a variety of war crimes and crimes against humanity. ICC PROSECUTOR WHOSE NETANYAHU WARRANT FUELED MAMDANI ARREST THREAT IS FIRED OVER SEXUAL MISCONDUCT Khan’s ICC only sought to grant "selective justice" according to legal expert Elliot Malin, who told Fox News Digital that he filed two cases with the Office of the Prosecutor in 2025 requesting warrants against the leaders he accuses of truly practicing war crimes, including genocide, in Israel and Gaza. Malin, president of Stratos Council, filed his first case with the ICC in Sept. 2025. It requested that the court investigate and issue warrants for two Iranian officials for "crimes against humanity, war crimes and genocide committed in Israel and Gaza on and after Oct. 7, 2023." Malin said that "It is very clear that the Islamic Republic is the principal to these proxies who are operating as agents of the regime… and we should hold the Islamic Republic directly accountable." The request for investigation and warrants was filed on behalf of Shnaider, whose filings say he has lost five generations of his family "to acts committed with the intent to destroy Jews," including the Holocaust. MIKE WALTZ FIGHTS BACK TEARS REVEALING WHAT HAMAS HOSTAGE REFUSED TO DO BEFORE RELEASE On Oct. 7, Shnaider told Fox News Digital that he turned on the news to see his niece, Shiri Bibas, "being taken away" with her young children into captivity. Bibas and her children were later murdered as hostages. Shnaider says that he prays that Bibas "didn’t witness how they did what they did to a four-year-old and a nine-month-old." Shnaider’s sister and brother-in-law were also murdered at Kibbutz Nir Oz on Oct. 7. He explained that they "were burned inside the house in a brutal way that you cannot imagine, you cannot explain, you cannot answer." By the time of his sister and brother-in-law’s burial, he explained that "there was hardly anything left" to put in the caskets. Shnaider says that the grief from the horrific losses of his family on Oct. 7 "doesn’t compute in my body," leaving him "choking" with tears. Though Shnaider acknowledges that he will never understand the rationale behind hate, he said that "the most I can do is fight them in the way I can." He believes it is now up to the ICC "to put a stop to it." If the ICC fails to do so, Shnaider says the court "should be condemned" for its bias. While the case against Iranian leaders was filed on behalf of just the Shnaider family, Malin advocates filing a case on behalf of each family who lost relatives during the attacks of Oct. 7. In Dec. 2025, Malin filed a second case, requesting investigation and arrest warrants for over a dozen Hamas members for a myriad of "war crimes, and crimes against humanity committed against Palestinians in Gaza." IDF PUSHES BACK ON CLAIM IT TARGETS JOURNALISTS IN GAZA, SAYS 170 WERE PART OF TERROR GROUPS, INCLUDING HAMAS Malin says it is also important to hold Hamas leaders "directly accountable for the crime of genocide." He explained that Hamas attackers’ own words prove that there was no military goal during the Oct. 7 attacks, which largely killed civilians. Malin said Hamas attackers told Oct. 7 victims that they would continue attacks into Israel "until there are no Jews left in Palestine," and during phone calls to family, an attacker celebrated specifically having killed Jews. "They’re not talking about soldiers. They’re not talking about people who, in the course of combat or conflict, would be allowed to be targeted. They’re talking about civilians," Malin said. Malin added that the individuals now trying to justify Hamas’ actions on Oct. 7 "are now justifying the actual crime of genocide." The case against Hamas leaders also notes their particular role in the deaths of innocent Gazans during the conflict that followed Oct. 7. "The goal there is to raise light of Hamas’ criminal conduct against Palestinians in Gaza," Malin said. He pointed out Hamas’ use of civilians as human shields and their torture of civilians, which he says "we have years of evidence for." Malin said that the ICC has not responded to either of the cases he has filed. "If we don’t shed light on that at the ICC and the ICC refuses to do anything about it, then the only question for me… is what is the purpose that you serve?" TRUMP ADMINISTRATION SANCTIONS SITTING PRESIDENT OF THE INTERNATIONAL CRIMINAL COURT FOR 'ABUSES OF POWER' Malin argues that though the Iranian officials, one of whom was killed during the ongoing conflict with the U.S., were from a state that is not party to the statute, because the ICC has jurisdiction over Gaza, it is responsible for overseeing crimes committed there. In response to questions about their response to Malin’s filings, the Office of the Prosecutor for the ICC told Fox News Digital, "On the Situation in the State of Palestine the Office of the Prosecutor (OTP) is actively investigating all crimes committed within the Court’s jurisdiction since 13 June 2014. The investigation is ongoing, and the Office continues to collect evidence in that context." The statement added, "The OTP carries out its mandate independently and impartially, in accordance with its founding treaty, the Rome Statute," it continued. "The Office does not disclose details of the investigation to ensure the integrity of its processes and proceedings and to maintain the safety and security of all concerned, including victims, witnesses, the Office's staff and all those who cooperate with the Office and support its activities." Malin said that Khan sought warrants against senior Israeli and Hamas leaders for the crime against humanity of extermination, which he described as "genocide without the intent [to commit genocide.]" CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP That warrant was denied for Israeli leaders, but ultimately approved for Deif, though he had been previously killed in an Israeli air strike. Earlier this month, Secretary of State Marco Rubio imposed sweeping financial sanctions against the court. In a recorded video, Rubio charged, "Our message is clear: The United States and the American people are not subject to the jurisdiction of this fake ICC."
